meta.titre: Economic Development: features of underdevelopment and how growth differs from development
meta.sous_theme: Growth versus development, underdevelopment and its indicators

sections.contenu_markdown: A new highway, a modern hospital and a big factory change the look of a country. But does a child in a remote village go to school, drink clean water and see a doctor when sick? Governments and teachers talk about development because it concerns the lives of ordinary people and not only the national income. In the GCE paper, students must list the features of an underdeveloped economy, tell growth from development and use simple figures to compare countries.

items: Gross domestic product (GDP) is the value of all goods and services produced in a country in a year.
Income per head is the total income divided by the number of people.
A raw material, such as timber or crude oil, is a primary product that has not yet been processed.
Savings are income not spent on consumption.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Growth and development
**Economic growth** is an increase in a country's real output (GDP) over time. It is measured as a percentage change:

$$\text{Growth rate} = \frac{\text{new GDP} - \text{old GDP}}{\text{old GDP}} \times 100$$

Real means adjusted for price changes. GDP per head is GDP divided by the population. **Economic development** is wider: it means a lasting rise in the living standards of ordinary people, including better incomes, health, education, housing and jobs. Growth can happen without development if the gains go to only a few people.

### Characteristics of an underdeveloped economy
Underdeveloped countries are also called developing or less developed countries.

| Area | Typical features |
|---|---|
| Income and production | Low income per head; heavy dependence on farming and on exports of raw materials; little industry |
| Capital | Low savings and investment, so few machines and factories |
| Labour | Unemployment and underemployment; many workers with little training |
| Population | High birth rates, fast population growth and a large share of young dependants |
| Social conditions | Low life expectancy, poor health care, lower literacy, poor housing and malnutrition |
| Infrastructure | Poor roads, unreliable electricity and water supply |
| Distribution | Wide gaps between rich and poor |

### Measuring development
Economists use income per head, life expectancy, the literacy rate, infant mortality and access to clean water. The Human Development Index combines income, health and education in one figure.

### Vicious circle of poverty
Low income leads to low saving, which leads to low investment, then to low productivity and back to low income. Breaking the circle needs investment, education and health care, better infrastructure, a wider range of exports and sound government. Some countries also use family planning to slow population growth.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks for two or more characteristics
variantes.contenu_markdown: Write each characteristic as a short, separate statement and keep to the number requested. Choose clear features such as low income per head or a high birth rate.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks to distinguish or to explain
variantes.contenu_markdown: Define growth as a rise in output, define development as a rise in living standards, and add that growth can occur without development when only a few people gain.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When GDP and population figures are given
variantes.contenu_markdown: Divide GDP by population to get GDP per head. To compare years, take the change, divide by the starting figure and multiply by 100. Watch the units: a billion is a thousand million.

sections.enonce_markdown:
In a certain country, real GDP in year 1 is 6,000 billion FCFA and the population is 20 million. In year 2, real GDP is 6,300 billion FCFA and the population is 20.4 million.
(a) Calculate the growth rate of GDP.
(b) Calculate GDP per head in each year.
(c) Calculate the percentage change in GDP per head.
(d) Explain why GDP growth alone does not prove development.

etapes.action: Find the growth rate of GDP.
etapes.justification: Change in GDP divided by the old GDP, times 100.

etapes.action: Find GDP per head in year 1.
etapes.justification: Divide GDP by population, in the same units.

etapes.action: Find GDP per head in year 2.
etapes.justification: Same method with the new figures.

etapes.action: Find the change in GDP per head.
etapes.justification: Population grew too, so per head growth is smaller than GDP growth.
Development concerns the living standards of ordinary people.
etapes.resultat_markdown: An average figure hides who gets the extra income. Health, education and the share of income received by the poor must also improve.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) 5%. (b) 300,000 FCFA and about 308,824 FCFA. (c) About 2.9%. (d) GDP growth shows more output but not whether health, education and living conditions of ordinary people have improved.

items.erreur_markdown: "Economic growth and economic development mean exactly the same thing."
items.pourquoi_faux: Growth is a rise in output. Development includes better health, education and living conditions.
items.correction_markdown: Growth means more output; development means a lasting improvement in the standard of living of the population. Growth is needed for development but is not enough.

items.pourquoi_faux: Many have plenty of resources but lack the capital, skills and technology to use them.
items.correction_markdown: The problem is often that resources are unused or exported as raw materials, not that they are absent.

items.erreur_markdown: "A country with a very large GDP must be developed."
items.pourquoi_faux: A large population can share a large GDP and still have a low income per head. Wide gaps between rich and poor also matter.
items.correction_markdown: Use GDP per head and other indicators such as life expectancy and literacy to judge development.

items.erreur_markdown: "One characteristic of underdevelopment is a very large industrial sector."
items.pourquoi_faux: This describes a more developed economy.
items.correction_markdown: An underdeveloped economy depends heavily on farming and raw material exports and has little industry.

items.pourquoi_faux: The ratio is upside down. Income per person must come from dividing the total by the number of people.

items.enonce_markdown: State four characteristics of an underdeveloped economy.
items.solution_markdown: Any four of: **low income per head**; **heavy dependence on farming and raw material exports**; **high birth rate and fast population growth**; **high unemployment and underemployment**; **low savings and investment**; **poor infrastructure**; **low literacy and poor health care**.

items.enonce_markdown:
The real GDP of a country was 4,500 billion FCFA in 2020 and 4,680 billion FCFA in 2021. The population stayed at 18 million.
(a) Calculate the growth rate of GDP.
(b) Calculate GDP per head in each year.
(c) State by how much GDP per head rose.

Suppose country P has an income per head of 1,200,000 FCFA a year, life expectancy of 52 years and a literacy rate of 60%. Country Q has an income per head of 900,000 FCFA a year, life expectancy of 68 years and a literacy rate of 92%.
(a) Calculate by what percentage P's income per head is above Q's.
(b) Say which country is likely to be more developed and why.
(c) Explain why income per head alone can be a poor measure of development.
(d) Suggest two policies P could adopt.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\frac{1\,200\,000 - 900\,000}{900\,000} \times 100 =$ **33.3%** higher.
(b) **Q** is likely to be more developed, because its people live longer and more of them can read, even though the average income is lower.
(c) Income per head is only an average. It does not show how income is shared, nor the quality of health care, education and housing.
(d) Spend more on health care and schools, and improve roads and electricity to attract investment.

items_markdown: Economic growth is a rise in real output; economic development is a lasting rise in the living standards of the people.
Underdeveloped economies have low income per head, depend on farming and raw materials, and have little industry.
They also show high birth rates, unemployment, low savings and investment, poor infrastructure and low literacy.
Growth rate = change in GDP divided by the old GDP, times 100; GDP per head = GDP divided by population.
Income per head is not enough: life expectancy, literacy and the Human Development Index give a wider picture.
The vicious circle of poverty runs from low income to low saving, low investment and low productivity.
